Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'Being looked at sexually' is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision as the index trauma, especially when no other selected items suggest sexual trauma, harassment, or body-focused threat. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for signs that someone is entering the home implies an interpersonal intrusion/assault threat, which does not fit well with a motor vehicle collision and is not supported by the other items. The rest of the threat profile is general hypervigilance to sudden sounds, making this specific home-intruder monitoring item clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes usually implies clothing cues tied to the trauma context. For a motor vehicle collision, this is difficult to justify unless other items indicate clothing-specific trauma reminders, which they do not. It also does not connect plausibly to the selected triggers, which are taste, workplace, and sexual objectification.

Workplace as a trigger is weakly grounded for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision given the rest of the profile: the other trigger and threat items are sensory/accident-related, but nothing in appraisals, threat, or strategies explains why the workplace itself would be a salient trauma cue. This makes the trigger set less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste linked to a motor vehicle collision is possible but clinically unusual, and here it is unsupported by memory content or appraisals that would make a gustatory cue understandable. With no memory items and otherwise sound/crash/vehicle-focused content, this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, a specific taste trigger and an alcohol smell trigger are not impossible, but in combination they imply trauma details (e.g. ingestion, blood, alcohol involvement, hospital/chemical context) that are unsupported by the rest of the profile. The rest of the triggers, threat items, and appraisals are centered on vehicle crash/sound danger, so these sensory triggers look clinically disconnected from the trauma representation described elsewhere.

Undereating as a coping strategy is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links triggers, threat, negative appraisals, and avoidance-based coping around crash-related distress; avoid-driving and screen escape fit that pattern, but food restriction addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, memory, or appraisals. In this profile it appears clinically mismatched rather than a coherent extension of the same trauma-linked cycle.

vignette:
Tariq is a 30-year-old Middle Eastern man who works as a tax inspector, recently divorced, and who presented to the clinic several months after surviving a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. He was a passenger in a car driven by a friend who, Tariq later learned, had been drinking. The crash occurred at an intersection when the other driver ran a red light; the impact was sudden, the sound of crumpling metal and shattering glass immediate and total. Tariq remembers the sharp smell of alcohol in the enclosed car just before impact, the way the airbag struck his face, and the particular make and colour of the vehicle that hit them - a dark sedan not unlike dozens he passes each week. He survived with physical injuries that have since healed, but the psychological aftermath has not followed the same trajectory.

In the weeks following the collision, Tariq began noticing that certain sensory details from that evening had not stayed in the past where he felt they belonged. The smell of alcohol - encountered at a colleague's retirement gathering, or drifting from a restaurant he passed on his lunch break - would pull him back to the moment before impact with a vividness that felt less like memory and more like recurrence. Seeing cars with similar damage at the roadside, or vehicles resembling the one that struck them, produced the same effect. These triggers arrived without warning and, when they did, Tariq found himself scanning the environment with an intensity he could not switch off - hyperalert to every sudden sound, braced for impacts that did not come. He began startling badly at ordinary noises: a door slamming in the open-plan office where he reviews tax files, a colleague dropping a folder, a car horn from the street below. The threat felt omnipresent, and the triggers that reactivated his fear only confirmed to him that danger could arrive from any direction at any moment.

What compounded everything was what Tariq had come to believe about himself in the aftermath. He was certain, with a quiet but devastating conviction, that he was no longer capable of the things that had defined him - the focused, methodical competence he had built his professional identity around. He had once prided himself on reliability and self-sufficiency; now he could not trust his own reactions, his own steadiness, his own mind. He felt his emotional life had gone somewhere unreachable, flattened into a numbness that frightened him almost as much as the flashbacks. These appraisals did not remain passive - they actively sharpened his vigilance, as though his belief that he could no longer rely on himself demanded that he compensate by watching everything more carefully. And they made the triggers feel more potent: when a dark sedan pulled alongside him at a pedestrian crossing, the internal voice that said you cannot handle this amplified the sensory jolt into something close to paralysis.

Avoidance became the architecture of his days. He stopped driving entirely and refused to be a passenger in any vehicle, which in practical terms meant he began arriving late to field audits, offering implausible explanations to supervisors, and quietly withdrawing from cases that required travel. He had not told anyone at work what had happened. To fill the hours when he was not working, and to keep the images from surfacing, he spent long stretches on his phone - games, forums, streaming - anything that occupied enough of his attention to forestall the intrusions. He ate less and less, not from nausea but from a kind of punishing indifference to his own needs. Over time, these strategies, which had initially offered brief relief, began feeding back into the very beliefs they were meant to quiet. Each hour lost to a screen, each meal skipped, each journey refused, confirmed to Tariq that he was diminished - less capable, less present, less himself - and that confirmation kept him hyperalert, braced, scanning.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at work when a colleague knocked over a metal wastepaper bin and Tariq, in front of three people, dropped to a crouch behind his desk. The shame of it was acute. He came to the clinic saying he was not sure he could be fixed, but that he could not continue living in a body that treated every ordinary afternoon as a crash site.
